title: Virtualization with VirtualBox and VMware

spans.text: Virtualization creates separate software-based computers inside one physical computer. The physical system is the host, the system inside it is the guest, and the environment is a virtual machine (VM). A VM receives CPU time, RAM, and a virtual disk. It is useful for learning, testing software, and building labs, but consumes host resources and is not a backup.

Check for Intel VT-x or AMD-V support. UEFI/BIOS may offer Intel Virtualization Technology, SVM Mode, or a similar setting; record the old value first. Leave RAM and disk space for the host. Hyper-V/VBS can affect compatibility with another hypervisor.

Download VirtualBox only from virtualbox.org. Get the OS ISO from its official source. Choose New, name the VM, select its OS type, assign RAM/CPU while keeping resources for the host, and create a virtual disk. Boot from the ISO and complete setup. Eject the ISO and restart the VM when done.

Download the host-matching Workstation Pro installer from VMware’s official site. Choose Create a New Virtual Machine, select the official ISO and guest OS, create its virtual disk, and assign reasonable RAM/CPU. Start the VM and finish guest installation; menus vary by release, so use the official guide.

NAT lets a VM use the host’s internet; Bridged makes it a separate network device and should not be used on an organization network without permission; Host-only creates a private host-to-VM network. A snapshot can restore an earlier state but may be lost if its disk fails, so keep a separate backup. Shared folders and clipboard can move data to the host.
